title: No-Data Rule Execution
background:
The `Rule` class in Json.Logic represents a self-contained computation. When a rule is built entirely from literal values and operators, it requires no external data to produce a result. `RuleExtensions.Apply()` is a convenience extension method that calls `rule.Apply(null)` — no data argument required.

The `JsonLogic` class provides static factory methods that return typed `Rule` objects. Primitive C# values such as `int`, `decimal`, `bool`, and `string` implicitly convert to `Rule` via conversion operators defined on the `Rule` base class, so you can pass literals directly to factory methods without calling `JsonLogic.Literal` explicitly.
instructions: Build a rule that adds the `a` and `b` test values, then return the result of `rule.Apply()`.

title: One-Call Rule Evaluation
background:
`JsonLogic.Apply(JsonNode? rule, JsonNode? context)` is the primary entry point for evaluating rules that arrive as raw JSON — from config files, databases, or API payloads. The rule is a `JsonNode?` whose single-key object structure identifies the operator; the context is the data the rule runs against. The library resolves the operator string, dispatches to the registered handler, and returns a `JsonNode?` result.

This model-less path requires no deserialization to typed `Rule` objects. You pass JSON in, you get JSON out. This makes it well-suited for scenarios where rules are fully external and the application just needs to execute them.
instructions: Evaluate the provided `rule` against the provided `data` using the model-less evaluation API, and return the result.

title: Typed Rule Composition
background:
Instead of writing rule JSON by hand, Json.Logic provides static factory methods on the `JsonLogic` class that build typed `Rule` objects directly in C#. These methods accept other `Rule` objects as arguments and return a new `Rule`. Primitive C# values implicitly convert to `Rule` via `LiteralRule`, so literal values can be passed without an explicit wrapper.

Once composed, the rule is evaluated by calling `rule.Apply(data)` where `data` is a `JsonNode?`. The typed path is well-suited for application code where rules are constructed programmatically rather than loaded from external JSON.
instructions: Build a typed rule that returns `true` only when `age` is greater than 18 and less than 65, then apply it to the test data.

title: Rule Deserialization
background:
Rules stored as JSON strings — in a database, config file, or API response — can be deserialized directly to a typed `Rule` using `System.Text.Json`. The library registers a `JsonConverter<Rule>` (`LogicComponentConverter`) that handles the conversion. A single-key JSON object is read as an operator rule; a multi-key object or primitive becomes a `LiteralRule`; a JSON array becomes a `RuleCollection`.

Once deserialized, the `Rule` is a first-class typed object you can evaluate with `rule.Apply(data)`, inspect, or serialize back to JSON. This makes it straightforward to load rules from any storage format and execute them in a strongly-typed context.
instructions: Deserialize `test["rule"]` to a typed `Rule`, then apply it to `test["data"]`.

title: Variable Resolution
background:
`JsonLogic.Variable(string path)` creates a `var` rule that reads a value from the data object at a dot-delimited path. When the path is not found in the data, the rule returns `null`. `JsonLogic.Variable(string path, Rule defaultValue)` provides a fallback: the default is returned whenever the path resolves to nothing, avoiding a `null` result without extra null checks in the calling code.

The default value parameter accepts a `Rule`, but because `string` and other primitive types implicitly convert to `Rule`, you can pass a plain string literal directly. This makes variable access with fallbacks concise and readable.
instructions: Build a variable lookup rule for the `city` path with a default of `"unknown"`, then apply it to the test data.

title: Truthiness
background:
Json.Logic defines its own truthiness semantics through the `IsTruthy()` extension method on `JsonNode?` (in the `Json.Logic` namespace). These rules drive the behavior of `And`, `Or`, `Not`, `If`, and other conditional operators throughout the library.

The falsey values are: `null`, `false`, `0`, `""` (empty string), `[]` (empty array), and `{}` (empty object). Everything else is truthy. The empty object being falsey is a notable difference from JavaScript; it is worth checking explicitly when writing integration code that passes objects through conditional rules.
instructions: Return whether `test["value"]` is truthy using the `IsTruthy()` extension method.

title: Strict vs Loose Equality
background:
Json.Logic provides two equality modes. `JsonLogic.StrictEquals` (the `===` operator) compares by both type and value: the number `1` and the string `"1"` are not equal. `JsonLogic.LooseEquals` (the `==` operator) coerces values through `Numberify` before comparing: `"1"` is parsed as `1`, making them equal.

Choosing the wrong mode is a common source of integration bugs. Strict equality is the safer default when you control the data shape. Loose equality is useful when rules may receive mixed types from external sources — for example, form fields that arrive as strings — and numeric equivalence is the intended comparison.
instructions: Build an equality rule that uses strict comparison when `test["strict"]` is `true` and loose comparison otherwise, using `a` and `b` from the test. Apply it with no data.

title: Numeric Coercion
background:
The arithmetic operators in Json.Logic — `Add`, `Subtract`, `Multiply`, `Divide`, `Modulus`, `Max`, and `Min` — pass each operand through a `Numberify()` conversion before computing. `Numberify` converts: `true` → `1`, `false` → `0`, `null` → `0`, parseable numeric strings like `"3"` → `3`, and non-parseable strings → `null` (which short-circuits the result to `null`).

This means that rules operating on data from external sources — where a field might be `"5"` or `5` depending on the sender — produce consistent arithmetic results without requiring the caller to normalize types in advance.
instructions: Build a numeric rule that sums `test["a"]` and `test["b"]`, then return the result of `rule.Apply()`.

title: Rule Logging
background:
`JsonLogic.Log(rule)` wraps any rule in a diagnostic pass-through. When applied, it evaluates the inner rule, writes the result to `Console.WriteLine`, and returns the value unchanged. The return value of a `Log` rule is identical to the return value of the inner rule, so it can be embedded anywhere in a rule tree without affecting evaluation.

This is the intended way to observe intermediate values during development. By wrapping a sub-expression in `Log`, you get visibility into what the rule is computing at that point without changing behavior or restructuring the rule tree.
instructions: Build a rule that adds `a` and `b`, wrap that rule in a logging rule, and return the result of `rule.Apply()`.

title: Rule Tree Serialization
background:
Every typed `Rule` built with the Json.Logic factory methods supports round-trip serialization. The `LogicComponentConverter` registered on `Rule` writes it back to its original operator-and-arguments JSON form. Deserializing that JSON with `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Rule>()` reconstructs an equivalent rule that evaluates identically.

This makes typed rules suitable for storage, caching, and transport. You can build a rule in C#, serialize it to a string, store it, load it back, and evaluate it — all without losing fidelity. The same `System.Text.Json` options apply throughout, so no extra configuration is needed.
instructions: Serialize `rule` to JSON, deserialize it back to a typed `Rule`, then apply the deserialized rule to `test["data"]`.

title: Unknown Operator Behavior
background:
The two evaluation paths in Json.Logic handle unknown operators differently. The model-less path — `JsonLogic.Apply(JsonNode? rule, ...)` — silently returns the original rule node unchanged when no handler is registered for the operator. The typed deserialization path — `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Rule>(...)` — throws a `JsonException` immediately at deserialization time because the converter cannot map the operator string to a registered `Rule` type.

This distinction matters when building integration code that accepts rules from external sources. The typed path fails fast and is straightforward to reason about; the model-less path is permissive and requires you to inspect the result if you need to detect unrecognized operators.
instructions: Try to deserialize `test["rule"]` as a `Rule` and apply it to `test["data"]`. Catch `JsonException` and return `null` if the operator is unknown.

title: Custom Operator (Model-less)
background:
The model-less evaluation path supports custom operators through `RuleRegistry.AddRule(string op, IRule rule)`. You implement the `IRule` interface — a single `Apply(JsonNode? args, EvaluationContext context)` method — and register an instance against an operator name string. Once registered, any call to `JsonLogic.Apply` that encounters that operator will dispatch to your handler.

Inside the handler, `args` is the raw JSON argument from the rule, and you can call `JsonLogic.Apply(args, context)` to evaluate it recursively. This allows your operator to accept nested rules as its argument, just like the built-in operators do.
instructions: Implement an `IRule` handler for a `"double"` operator that multiplies its evaluated argument by 2, then register it in the rule registry before evaluation.

title: Custom Rule Type
background:
For reusable, named C# types rather than anonymous `IRule` instances, you can extend the abstract `Rule` class directly. Subclassing `Rule` gives you a first-class C# type with a proper `Apply(JsonNode? data, JsonNode? contextData = null)` method. You accept other `Rule` objects via constructor injection for sub-expressions and evaluate them with `_inner.Apply(data, contextData)`.

Instances of your rule subclass compose freely with factory-built rules: `JsonLogic.And(myRule, JsonLogic.Variable("flag"))` works without any registration. The `contextData` parameter carries item-scope context from collection operators like `Map` and `Reduce`, so forwarding it to inner rules ensures correct behavior when your custom rule is nested inside those operators.
instructions: Implement a `DoubleRule : Rule` class that evaluates an inner rule and returns the numeric result multiplied by 2. Construct it with a rule that reads `x` from the test data, then apply it.
